title: What is known about 1RB1RA_0LC1LE_1LD1LC_1LA0LB_1LF1RE_---0RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RA_0LC1LE_1LD1LC_1LA0LB_1LF1RE_---0RA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape. It is the machine the bbchallenge community calls Antihydra, a cryptid: a machine whose halting is equivalent to an open Collatz-like problem.
Lean proves the equivalence here, for every step of the run: the machine halts from blank tape exactly when a simple arithmetic walk on two numbers reaches its halting case.
verdict: The question is open, and is now a question about numbers. Lean proves (halts_iff, kernel) that the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of (2, 7) under the map (p, a) ↦ (p + 2, 3k + 4) for a = 2k + 1, (p − 1, 3k + 2) for a = 2k ever meets an even a with p = 0.

Why nobody expects a halt. The parity of a behaves like a fair coin, so p is a random walk with steps +2 and −1 and an upward drift of ½ per step. After 106 steps of the walk (a computation, not a proof) p is 498,505; a walk of that kind started at height p ever reaches −1 with probability about 0.618p+1. Deciding it would need control of the parity sequence of ⌊3x/2⌋ iterates, a famously hard problem (Mahler's 3/2 problem is of this kind).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: The sweep and its two endings
claims.text: For every p, a, b, with Q p a b = 0^∞ 1^p 0 1^a 0 1^b B> 0^∞: Q p (a+3) (b+1) reaches Q p (a+1) (b+4) in 2b + 13 steps (one sweep: the middle block loses 2, the right block gains 3), and by induction k sweeps at once; a middle block of 1 gives Q (p+2) (c+4) 2 from Q p 1 (c+2), a middle block of 2 gives Q p (c+5) 2 from Q (p+1) 2 (c+2), and Q 0 2 (c+2) halts after c + 8 steps. The shift rules are generated from the table by bbtools.symtm and proved by rfl and the crossing lemmas.

claims.title: Halting is equivalent to the Antihydra walk
claims.text: After 62 steps from blank tape the run is at Q 2 7 2. With nxt (p, a) = (p + 2, 3k + 4) for a = 2k + 1, (p − 1, 3k + 2) for a = 2k and p ≥ 1, and no successor for a even and p = 0: the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of (2, 7) under nxt stops. Both directions: a stop gives a halting run; an orbit that never stops gives runs of every length.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 44,299 cells have been visited and 44,296 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The walk does not stop in its first 10<sup>6</sup> steps
claims.text: Python big integers iterate nxt from (2, 7) a million times: p never falls below 2 and ends at 498,505 (a then has 584,967 bits). The first 12 points agree with a direct simulation of the machine, cell for cell, at the step counts the Lean rules give (step 62, 173, 423, …, 1,405,109).

claims.title: Why a halt is not expected
claims.text: With x = a + 5 the map is x ↦ ⌊3x/2⌋, and p goes up 2 when x is even and down 1 when x is odd. If the parities are independent fair coins (they look so: no bias is known), p is a random walk with drift +½ per step; from height p it ever reaches −1 with probability φ<sup>−(p+1)</sup>, φ = (1+√5)/2, and p is already about 500,000. This is the bbchallenge community's reading too (Antihydra is listed as a cryptid, probviously non-halting).

claims.title: Does the walk ever stop?
claims.text: Open. Proving it never stops would need to show that the parities of the iterates of ⌊3x/2⌋ from x = 12 are not too often odd, an unsolved problem of the same kind as Mahler's 3/2 problem.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows whether it halts. Lean proves that this machine halts exactly when a simple walk on numbers does: a number is multiplied by 3/2 again and again, and a counter goes up 2 for every even result and down 1 for every odd one. The machine halts only if the counter ever drops below zero. It has climbed past 500,000 and keeps climbing, but nobody can prove it never comes back.

facts.text: Proved in Lean for the whole run, both directions.
No stop; the counter ends near 500,000.
The chance a fair ±walk like this ever comes back down.

sections.heading: Three blocks of ones and a sweeping head
html: Watch the run for a while and the tape settles into three blocks of 1s separated by single 0s, with the head bouncing at the right end. Write it as 1^p 0 1^a 0 1^b.

<text x="440" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">each sweep: 2 ones leave the middle, 3 join the right</text>
<text x="70" y="28" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">the counter</text><text x="273" y="28" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">the number</text>
</svg>

Each round trip of the head (a sweep, 2b + 13 steps) takes two 1s from the middle block and adds three to the right block. So while the middle block lasts, the right block grows by 3 for every 2 the middle loses: the middle number gets multiplied by 3/2.

When the middle block is down to one or two 1s, the head goes further left and touches the left block:

  • if a was odd (one 1 left), the left block gains 2;
  • if a was even (two 1s left), the left block loses 1 — and if there is no left block at all, the machine halts.

Then the right block becomes the new middle block, and a fresh right block of two 1s starts. In numbers: a = 2k + 1 gives (p + 2, 3k + 4), and a = 2k gives (p − 1, 3k + 2). The run from blank tape reaches (p, a) = (2, 7) after 62 steps, then (4, 13), (6, 22), (5, 35), (7, 55), (9, 85), …

sections.heading: A number times 3/2, and a counter that flips coins
html:
Set x = a + 5. Then each step is just x ↦ ⌊3x/2⌋, and the counter p goes up 2 when x is even and down 1 when x is odd. The machine halts if and only if p would go below 0. Lean checks this equivalence for the whole infinite run (halts_iff).

Nobody can predict the parity of ⌊3x/2⌋ iterates: they look like fair coin flips. If they are, p is a random walk with drift +½ per step, and once it is high it almost surely never returns. After a million steps p is near 500,000, and the chance of a walk like that ever coming back to −1 is about 0.618500,000. That is why the community calls Antihydra probviously non-halting, and why proving it is out of reach: it is a problem of the same kind as Mahler's 3/2 problem, open since 1968.
Try the walk. Start from the machine's own values or your own, and step it. The machine halts exactly when this says halt.

explainer.title: Antihydra: a Turing machine that is secretly a coin-flipping walk

summary: Antihydra: halts iff the walk x → ⌊3x/2⌋, with a counter +2 for even x and −1 for odd x, ever drives the counter below 0 (proved equivalent in Lean); open, and heuristically never.
